# Storybook rules

Apply these rules to every story file you write or review. The first section is always in force; open a file from the table when the task touches it.

## Always apply (critical, high)

### Take userEvent from the test function's parameters, never from an import

_critical · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Destructure `userEvent`, `canvas`, `canvasElement`, `args` and `step` from the parameters of the
`.test()` or `play` function. Import only `expect`, `fn`, `waitFor` and `screen` from
`storybook/test`.

**Why.** An imported `userEvent` is not wired into Storybook's instrumentation, so interactions run outside
its timing and do not show up in the interactions panel. The failures it causes are intermittent
and hard to trace back to the import.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
import { expect, fn, userEvent } from "storybook/test";

Story.test("Submits the form", async ({ canvas }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
import { expect, fn } from "storybook/test";

Story.test("Submits the form", async ({ canvas, userEvent }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
});
```

### Find elements the way a user or a screen reader does

_high · any_

**Rule.** Locate elements by their role and accessible name first, then by their label, then by visible
text. Reach for a test id or a selector only when the element has no accessible identity at all,
and treat that as a defect to fix in the component.

**Why.** A test that finds a button by its role and name keeps passing through any refactor that keeps the
button usable, and fails when a user could no longer find it. A test that finds it by class name or
test id breaks on harmless markup changes and stays green when the accessible name disappears.

### Query portal content through screen, not canvas

_high · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Trigger the interaction through `canvas`, then find the portal content through `screen`, which
queries the whole document. Use `canvas` for everything rendered inside the story root.

**Why.** Modals, popovers, tooltips and select option lists are portalled to `document.body`. A `canvas`
query never finds them, so the test fails with "unable to find role dialog" even though the dialog
is plainly on screen.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /open/i }));
const dialog = await canvas.findByRole("dialog");
```

**Correct:**

```ts
await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /open/i }));
const dialog = await screen.findByRole("dialog");
await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /close/i }));
```

### Attach independent checks to one story with .test(), not separate play stories

_high · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Write every independent assertion as its own `.test()` on the story that has the right args. Use
`play` only for a demo without assertions, or for one flow whose steps genuinely depend on each
other, grouped with `step()`.

**Why.** Separate stories per test multiply `meta.story()` boilerplate and fill the sidebar with copies of
the same state. Assertions packed into one `play` stop at the first failure, so one broken
behaviour hides the result of every check after it.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
export const SubmitClicked = meta.story({
  play: async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {
    await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
    await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
    await expect(canvas.getByRole("button")).toBeDisabled();
  },
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const FilledForm = meta.story({ args: { defaultValues: filled } });

FilledForm.test("Clicking submit calls onSubmit", async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
  await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
});

FilledForm.test("Disables submit while saving", async ({ canvas, userEvent }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
  await expect(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i })).toBeDisabled();
});
```

### Write stories with CSF Next factories, not CSF 3 objects

_high · storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Build every story through the chain `definePreview` → `preview.meta()` → `meta.story()`.
`definePreview` lives only in the Storybook preview file. A story file has no default export and
no hand-written `Meta` or `StoryObj` types. How the preview is imported and what the story file is
called depends on the framework; each framework has its own note implementing this one.

**Why.** CSF 3 objects (`satisfies Meta<typeof C>`, `export default meta`) cannot carry `.test()`, and
their types are annotated by hand, so they drift from the component's props. Mixing both formats
in one project makes every new story a guess.

### Put a React story next to its component and import the typed preview

_high · typescript, react, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Create `<component>.stories.tsx` in the component's folder. Import the preview with
`import preview from "~/.storybook/preview"` and build the meta with `preview.meta({ ... })`.
Export stories as `meta.story({ ... })` and let TypeScript infer every type.

**Why.** The typed preview is what makes `meta.story()` know the component's props. A story file that
imports `Meta` from the framework package falls back to CSF 3 and loses `.test()`.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from "@storybook/react-vite";

const meta = { component: SubmitButton } satisfies Meta<typeof SubmitButton>;
export default meta;
export const Primary: StoryObj<typeof meta> = {};
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
import preview from "~/.storybook/preview";

import { SubmitButton } from "./submit-button";

const meta = preview.meta({ title: "Components/Submit Button", component: SubmitButton });
export const SubmitButtonStory = meta.story({ name: "Submit Button" });
```

### Pick getBy, queryBy or findBy by what the assertion expects

_high · typescript, testing-library_

**Rule.** Use `getBy*` for an element that must already be on screen, `queryBy*` when the assertion is that
it is absent, and `findBy*` (or `waitFor`) for anything that appears after an interaction, a
request or an animation.

**Why.** `getBy*` throws before a `not.toBeInTheDocument()` assertion can run, so a negative check written
with it fails for the wrong reason. A `getBy*` on content that renders a tick later fails
intermittently, which reads as a flaky suite rather than a wrong query.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
await expect(canvas.getByRole("alert")).not.toBeInTheDocument();
await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /save/i }));
await expect(canvas.getByText(/saved/i)).toBeVisible();
```

**Correct:**

```ts
await expect(canvas.queryByRole("alert")).not.toBeInTheDocument();
await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /save/i }));
await expect(await canvas.findByText(/saved/i)).toBeVisible();
```
